newsitem.title: USA: New magazine aimed at Internet shoppers.
newsitem.headline: New magazine aimed at Internet shoppers.

text.p: All wired up and don't know where to go?

Such is the lament of many an online shopper. With more and more vendors offering their wares in online catalogues, Internet shoppers can buy clothing, books, food and electronics, using their computers as if they were traditional paper catalogues.
Now a new magazine hopes to attract computer-literate consumers, doing for online shopping what Consumer Reports and Good Housekeeping have done for shoppers at the mall.

Internet Shopper, published by Mecklermedia of Westport, Conn., plans to "tell you where and how to buy products on the Internet; how to research sources and direct you to where to do the buying," said Dan Rosenbaum, editor-in-chief of the fledgling publication.
There are now thousands of vendors offering wares online, from major catalogues to Mom and Pop ventures, but the market is tiny compared with traditional catalogue sales.

Of the items available for purchase online from direct marketers, catalogues or individual vendors, books and music comprise 21 percent, computers make up 17 percent, financial services 9 percent, gifts 7 percent, and clothing 7 percent, according to Vos, Gruppo and Cappel Inc. and SIMBA Information Inc., two consulting groups.
Audio and video equipment make up another 5 percent, automotive items 5 percent, and food 5 percent. The rest fall into various categories.

This year, online shoppers will spend about $1.25 billion, according to Jupiter Communications, a New York-based market research and consulting firm. Next year, that should almost double to $2.33 billion, rising to $7.3 billion by 2000.
By comparison, traditional catalogue sales are expected to reach $74.6 billion this year and $79.8 billion in 1997, according to the Direct Marketing Association Inc., an industry group.
"Even if (online shopping) grows to 2 percent of catalogue sales, it represents a major shift in how people are relating to product and the shopping process," Rosenbaum said.
A prototype of Internet Shopper is expected in December and the first quarterly issue should be on the newsstands by April, Rosenbaum said. The glossy magazine will cost about $4.
Just about the first of its type, Rosenbaum said Internet Shopper will look at and test sites and tell readers how good or bad they are.

Drawing from a well of about 100 product categories, each issue of Internet Shopper will look at eight to 12 types of goods and services. From this list, the magazine will name the best of the category and best of the month. At the end of the year, there will be a best site of the year, Rosenbaum said.

Internet Shopper will also move into new territory by offering a consumer advocacy column for those shopping online. "We hope to do some conflict resolutions, addressing rights of the consumer in the online world," he said.
Because online shopping is so new, in most cases less than a year old, legislation, postal regulations and consumer protections have often not kept up with the marketplace.
"It's an emerging thing, it moves so fast," Rosenbaum said of the online shopping world.
Rosenbaum said topics the first issue may look at include travel, autos, clothing, computer equipment, food and greeting cards. He would not be more specific.

Addressing concerns about the safety of using credit cards for online purchases, Rosenbaum said, "nothing happens online that doesn't happen in the real world... I feel the idea of Internet security is overblown, but you should be aware."
Today, all browser software programmes support special coding to protect a purchaser's credit card number, he said.
But as a general rule, shoppers should stick to established companies online. "As with any direct vendor, deal with those you know -- the reputable ones," Rosenbaum said.
"Not today, but probably tomorrow -- two to three years -- there will be nothing that can't be bought online," he said.
